extracted.intended_audience: general readers and writers of literary/philosophical essays; critics and students of creative writing
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing imaginative, essayistic prose that combines autobiography, argument, and narrative 'romance' — aimed at persuading general readers while preserving wonder and complexity. Emphasizes use of images and moral/psychological insights rather than purely deductive exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrange argument as a riddle and its answer
rubrics_metrics.description: This book is arranged upon the positive principle of a riddle and its answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer structuring an affirmative philosophical work by first presenting puzzling personal reflections or questions and then showing how they are satisfied by your thesis; use surprise and revelation rather than only systematic proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use mental pictures rather than deductions
rubrics_metrics.description: I have attempted in a vague and personal way, in a set of mental pictures rather than in a series of deductions, to state the philosophy in which I have come to believe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor evocative images and anecdotal scenes to illustrate philosophical points instead of long abstract logical chains; let concrete pictures carry the argument to readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: State what you do NOT propose to prove
rubrics_metrics.description: Any one setting out to dispute anything ought always to begin by saying what he does not dispute... he should always state what he does not propose to prove.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At the start of an argumentative essay, explicitly declare the shared assumptions and the limits of your inquiry so readers know the common ground and the scope of your claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advocate an active imaginative life (romance)
rubrics_metrics.description: The thing I do not propose to prove... is this desirability of an active and imaginative life, picturesque and full of a poetical curiosity... we need this life of practical romance; the combination of something that is strange with something that is secure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write in a way that fosters the mixture of wonder and welcome: invite curiosity and imaginative engagement while providing moral or emotional security for the reader; treat romance as a moral and psychological need, not mere ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin by accepting shared values to connect with readers
rubrics_metrics.description: The thing I propose to take as common ground between myself and any average reader, is this desirability of an active and imaginative life...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start from propositions likely to be accepted by your intended audience to build rapport and make your further, more distinctive claims persuasive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be autobiographical when affirming a creed
rubrics_metrics.description: This book is unavoidably affirmative and therefore unavoidably autobiographical... it is the purpose of the writer to attempt an explanation... of how he personally has come to believe it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When giving a positive defense of a belief or philosophy, use personal anecdote and confession to lend sincerity and concreteness to abstract claims; modest self-reference can enhance credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mere paradox and light sophistry
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere light sophistry is the thing that I happen to despise most of all things... I know nothing so contemptible as a mere paradox; a mere ingenious defence of the indefensible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on clever paradoxes for their own sake or as a substitute for sincere argument; ensure wit serves truth and conviction rather than being an intellectual trick.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer wonder produced by a normal protagonist
rubrics_metrics.description: The old fairy tale makes the hero a normal human boy; it is his adventures that are startling; they startle him because he is normal. But in the modern psychological novel the hero is abnormal... Hence the fiercest adventures fail to affect him adequately, and the book is monotonous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For narrative impact, present a fundamentally ordinary or sane protagonist encountering extraordinary events — the contrast produces genuine wonder; avoid centering stories on protagonists who are already abnormal in ways that dull reader astonishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagination is not dangerous; avoid blaming creativity
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a notion adrift everywhere that imagination, especially mystical imagination, is dangerous to man's mental balance. Poets are commonly spoken of as psychologically unreliable... Facts and history utterly contradict this view. Most of the very great poets have been not only sane, but extremely business-like.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage imaginative thinking and poetic modes in writing; do not treat imagination as inherently pathological — excesses of purely analytical reason are the more likely danger.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware over-reliance on logic (the compressing tendency of reason)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exactly what does breed insanity is reason... The poet only desires exaltation and expansion, a world to stretch himself in. The logician who seeks to get the heavens into his head. And it is his head that splits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid reducing complex human experience to a single systematic explanation; keep room in your prose for openness, expansion, and the poetic rather than exclusively analytic precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid single thin explanations carried to excess
rubrics_metrics.description: The madman's explanation... is quite as complete as the sane one, but it is not so large... The strongest and most unmistakable MARK of madness is this combination between a logical completeness and a spiritual contraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not let one tidy theory explain everything in your work; cultivate breadth of perspective and resist the temptation to make an argument 'complete' at the cost of excluding other human realities — anti-pattern: narrow universality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value healthy hesitation and complexity in perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: He is without healthy hesitation and healthy complexity... we should be chiefly concerned not so much to give it arguments as to give it air, to convince it that there was something cleaner and cooler outside the suffocation of a single argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow ambivalence, nuance, and multiple threads in argument and narrative; use complexity as a virtue that makes characters and ideas believable and humane.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor manifold, miscellaneous presentation over reductive simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: The Christian admits that the universe is manifold and even miscellaneous, just as a sane man knows that he is complex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In exposition and storytelling, include disparate, apparently minor details and varied human traits — these miscellaneous elements enlarge the work and make it more true to life; avoid overly tidy, reductive schemes that flatten variety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be candid about failed claims to originality (humble tone)
rubrics_metrics.description: When I fancied that I stood alone I was really in the ridiculous position of being backed up by all Christendom... I did try to be original; but I only succeeded in inventing all by myself an inferior copy of the existing traditions of civilized religion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt humility in tone, acknowledging influences and the tradition behind ideas; candid self-mockery can disarm critics and make affirmative claims more persuasive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use everyday observation and small accidents as sources of insight
rubrics_metrics.description: How the flowers of the field or the phrases in an omnibus, the accidents of politics or the pains of youth came together in a certain order to produce a certain conviction...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mine ordinary life, small images, and chance observations for philosophical or narrative insight; grounding big claims in commonplace detail strengthens plausibility and reader connection.
